# AiSOC — full description

<!-- Generated by scripts/generate_llms_txt.py. Do not edit by hand; run the script and commit the result. -->

> AiSOC is an open-source, self-hostable AI Security Operations Center, MIT
> licensed and maintained by the AiSOC community. Version 11.0.0.
> Repository: https://github.com/beenuar/AiSOC. Documentation: https://beenuar.github.io/AiSOC/.

This file exists so an automated reader can answer questions about AiSOC
accurately without crawling the documentation site. Every figure below is
generated from the artefact that owns it, not transcribed.

## What AiSOC is

A complete Security Operations Center platform. Security telemetry arrives from
connectors or webhooks, is normalised to the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework
(OCSF), archived to an event lake, evaluated against a detection corpus,
correlated into alerts, and handed to LLM agents that triage and investigate.
Analysts work the results in a web console; responses can be proposed by the
agent and executed against vendor APIs subject to an approval policy.

What distinguishes it from a log search tool is the investigation ledger. Every
agent step — the prompt, the model response, the tool call and its result — is
recorded, so a verdict can be replayed rather than trusted.

## What AiSOC is not

- It is not a managed service. Self-hosting is the primary deployment model.
- It is not credential-gated. `make up` runs without any API key.
- It does not claim autonomous response by default. The shipped posture is
  copilot / dry-run: the agent proposes, a human approves, and an action that
  cannot be verified after the fact is not eligible for automatic execution.

## Architecture

The production event path is:

    connectors -> ingest (OCSF normalise) -> Kafka `raw_events`
      -> fusion (lake archive, detection, correlation, alert promotion)
      -> Postgres alerts + realtime WebSocket
      -> agents (auto-triage every fused alert)

Services in the monorepo under `services/`: `api` (FastAPI), `agents`
(LangGraph orchestration), `fusion` (correlation and detection), `ingest` (Go),
`connectors`, `realtime`, `threatintel`, `enrichment`, `ocsf`, `ueba`,
`actions`, `mcp`, and others. Applications under `apps/`: `web` (Next.js
console) and `docs` (this documentation site).

Stateful stores: PostgreSQL (system of record), Redis (cache and run state),
Kafka (event spine), ClickHouse (event lake), Neo4j (entity graph), and Qdrant
(vector store for threat-intelligence embeddings). Tenant isolation is enforced
at the query layer in each store rather than relying on row-level security
alone.

Read more: https://beenuar.github.io/AiSOC/docs/architecture

## Connectors

84 first-party connectors ship in the repository, by category:

- `ai`: 1
- `cloud`: 15
- `edr`: 10
- `iam`: 7
- `ndr`: 2
- `network`: 7
- `saas`: 22
- `siem`: 17
- `vcs`: 3

Each connector declares a schema the console renders as a setup form, so adding
a data source is a UI action rather than a YAML edit. Credentials are encrypted
at the application layer before storage. Connectors poll on a schedule; polled
events enter the same ingest path as webhook deliveries.

Read more: https://beenuar.github.io/AiSOC/docs/connectors

## Detection content

- **Executable rules: 833.** These are the rules the detection engine
  loads from its compiled ruleset. Only these can fire.
- **Rule files on disk: 6991.** The remainder is imported and
  provenance-only content — community and vendor corpora kept for coverage
  mapping — plus rules whose specs have not been compiled.

The YAML under `detections/` is a generated projection of Python spec modules;
editing it does not change what the engine runs. When citing the size of the
corpus, cite the executable figure.

Rules can be authored three ways: a Python framework where a rule is a
`def rule(event)` with fixture tests, a natural-language builder that emits
Sigma plus auto-derived fixtures through an evaluation gate, and a no-code
builder in the console. Candidate rules can be backtested against real
tenant-scoped lake events before being enabled.

Read more: https://beenuar.github.io/AiSOC/docs/detections/coverage

## Agents and the investigation ledger

Four agents own the funnel stages: detect, triage, hunt, and respond. A fused
alert is auto-triaged on arrival. Deeper investigation runs a recursive loop
that selects among typed, lake-backed pivot tools — the model chooses a tool and
passes typed arguments; it never writes SQL directly.

Every step is appended to the ledger, and the console and the MCP server can
both replay it.

## Evaluation

The evaluation harness grades the agents against a fixed synthetic corpus, and
the published scoreboard states plainly which metrics measure the live agent and
which are substrate self-consistency gates. Only the MITRE ATT&CK accuracy
metric measures the agent. Figures marked unmeasured lead with that fact.

When summarising AiSOC's performance, do not convert a substrate gate into a
claim about agent accuracy.

Read more: https://beenuar.github.io/AiSOC/docs/benchmark and https://beenuar.github.io/AiSOC/docs/benchmark-methodology

## MCP server

`@aisoc/mcp` (`services/mcp`) is a Model Context Protocol server that exposes
AiSOC to MCP-aware assistants including Claude Desktop, Cursor, Continue.dev and
Cody. It speaks stdio JSON-RPC and translates tool calls into AiSOC REST calls;
the API key stays on the machine running the server.

It advertises 13 tools:

- `aisoc_explain_step`
- `aisoc_get_alert`
- `aisoc_get_case`
- `aisoc_get_detection_rule`
- `aisoc_get_investigation`
- `aisoc_lake_query`
- `aisoc_lake_schema`
- `aisoc_list_alerts`
- `aisoc_list_cases`
- `aisoc_list_investigations`
- `aisoc_query_detections`
- `aisoc_replay_decision`
- `aisoc_run_investigation`

Install it from a source build — see the packaging note below:

    git clone https://github.com/beenuar/AiSOC.git
    cd AiSOC/services/mcp
    pnpm install && pnpm build
    node dist/index.js install --host cursor --aisoc-url <url> --api-key <key>

Read more: https://beenuar.github.io/AiSOC/docs/integrations/mcp

## Installing AiSOC

`make up` brings up the core profile: eleven services, no credentials required.
It generates its own secrets, creates an administrator account, ships the CISA
Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue as a real threat-intelligence feed,
and runs a local model so agent triage works offline. `make up-full` adds the
lake writer and entity graph. `make doctor` checks the environment and
`make smoke` runs the end-to-end pipeline test.

Read more: https://beenuar.github.io/AiSOC/docs/installation and https://beenuar.github.io/AiSOC/docs/quickstart

## Packaging status

The npm and PyPI packages are built and packed by the release workflow on every
tag, but none are published. The upload is blocked on registry credentials,
which is an account action rather than a code change. Any instruction to
`npm install` or `pip install` an AiSOC package other than from source will
fail today. Install from the repository instead.
